stem: A web server runs on a machine with a single CPU core. It keeps 100 client connections open and makes progress on each of them by switching between them while others wait on the network. How is this best described?

options.text: Parallel but not concurrent, since requests overlap in time
options.why: Parallelism needs simultaneous execution on several cores; one core never runs two things at the same instant.

options.text: Concurrent but not parallel: tasks overlap in time on one core
options.why: Concurrency is about structuring work so tasks make progress over overlapping periods; parallelism is simultaneous execution.

options.text: Neither, because a single core can only handle one request
options.why: One core handles many requests by interleaving them; it just never executes two at the same instant.

options.text: Both concurrent and parallel, since 100 connections are active
options.why: Having many active connections does not create simultaneous execution without more cores.

explanation: Concurrency means several tasks are in progress during overlapping time periods; parallelism means they literally execute at the same instant on different hardware. A single core can be highly concurrent by interleaving work, especially I/O-bound work, but it cannot be parallel.
reference: Go blog: Concurrency is not parallelism (Rob Pike)

stem: Threads that belong to the same process share the process heap, but each thread has its own stack.

options.text: True
options.why: Threads share the address space (heap, globals, code, open files) but each gets a private stack and register set.

options.text: False
options.why: Separate stacks are what let each thread keep its own call chain and local variables.

explanation: All threads of a process see the same address space, which is why they can share data cheaply and also why they can race on it. Each thread still needs its own stack and saved registers so it can run its own sequence of calls.
reference: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, ch. 26 (Concurrency: An Introduction)

stem: Match each workload with the execution model that fits it best.

options.text: A pool of OS processes or native threads, one per core
options.why: CPU-bound work needs real parallelism across cores.

options.text: An event loop with non-blocking I/O
options.why: Many mostly-idle connections are cheap to multiplex on one thread.

options.text: A single thread, run sequentially
options.why: Short, dependent steps gain nothing from concurrency.

options.text: A thread pool sized well above the core count
options.why: Blocking I/O waits leave cores idle, so more threads than cores keep them busy.

prompts.text: Resizing millions of images, pure computation
A chat gateway holding 50,000 idle WebSocket connections
A 20 ms script that reads a config file and prints three values
A service that calls a legacy blocking SOAP API for every request

explanation: Match the model to where time is spent. CPU-bound work wants one worker per core. Huge numbers of idle connections want event-driven multiplexing. Blocking I/O wants more threads than cores so waits overlap. Tiny sequential jobs want no concurrency at all, because the overhead outweighs any gain.
reference: Goetz, Java Concurrency in Practice, §8.2 (Sizing thread pools)

stem: Which of these services gains the most from moving to a machine with twice as many CPU cores, assuming it is already written to use all available cores?

options.text: A reverse proxy that mostly waits on upstream responses
options.why: Its time goes to waiting on the network, so extra cores sit idle.

options.text: A video transcoder that keeps every core at 100%
options.why: CPU-bound work that is already parallel scales with core count.

options.text: A cron job that copies files between two network shares
options.why: The bottleneck is disk and network throughput, not CPU.

options.text: An API whose latency is dominated by slow database queries
options.why: More app cores do not make the database answer faster.

explanation: Extra cores help only CPU-bound work that can use them. I/O-bound services spend most of their time waiting, so their bottleneck is the network, disk or another service, and doubling cores changes little.
reference: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, ch. 7 (Scheduling: CPU and I/O bursts)

stem: A service receives 200 requests per second, and each request spends on average 50 ms inside the service. On average, how many requests are in the service at the same time? Type a number.
explanation: Little's law: L = λ × W = 200 req/s × 0.05 s = 10. On average 10 requests are in flight, so the service needs capacity (threads, connections, slots) for at least that many, plus headroom for bursts.
reference: Little's law (L = λW)

stem: 90% of a program's running time can be perfectly parallelised and 10% is strictly serial. Using Amdahl's law, roughly what speedup do 10 cores give?

options.text: About 9×, since 90% of the work speeds up
options.why: That ignores that the serial 10% still takes its full time.

options.text: About 10×, one unit of speedup per core
options.why: Linear speedup needs a serial fraction of zero.

options.text: About 5.3×, as the serial 10% dominates
About 1.9×, since only 10% stays serial
options.why: That treats the serial share as the bottleneck far too strongly.

explanation: Amdahl's law: speedup = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/n). With p = 0.9 and n = 10: 1 / (0.1 + 0.09) = 1 / 0.19 ≈ 5.26. Even a small serial fraction cuts the benefit sharply: here 10 cores deliver barely half of the ideal 10×.
reference: Amdahl, 'Validity of the single processor approach' (1967)

stem: 95% of a job's runtime is perfectly parallel. Under Amdahl's law, what is the maximum speedup possible, however many cores you add?

options.text: 95×, one per percent of parallel work
options.why: The limit comes from the serial part, not the parallel part.

options.text: 20×, set by the 5% serial fraction alone
options.why: The ceiling is 1 / (1 − p) = 1 / 0.05 = 20.

options.text: Unlimited, given enough cores
options.why: The serial 5% never shrinks, so speedup is bounded.

options.text: 1.05×, the inverse of the parallel fraction
options.why: That inverts the formula incorrectly.

explanation: As n → ∞ the parallel term p/n → 0, so speedup → 1 / (1 − p). With 5% serial work the job can never run more than 20× faster than on one core, which is why shrinking the serial fraction often matters more than adding hardware.
reference: Amdahl's law

stem: Which three are shared by all threads of the same process? (Choose three.)

options.text: The heap and global variables
options.why: All threads see the same address space, including heap allocations and globals.

options.text: Open file descriptors and sockets
options.why: Descriptors belong to the process, so any thread can use them.

options.text: The call stack and local variables
options.why: Each thread has its own stack, so locals are private unless their address escapes.

options.text: The program code (text segment)
options.why: All threads execute the same mapped code.

options.text: The program counter and CPU registers
options.why: Each thread has its own execution context, saved and restored on switches.

options.text: Thread-local storage variables
options.why: TLS gives each thread its own copy by design.

explanation: A process owns the address space and kernel resources: heap, globals, code, open files and sockets. A thread is an execution context inside it: its own stack, registers, program counter and thread-local storage. Sharing the first group is what makes threads cheap to communicate with, and also what makes data races possible.
reference: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, ch. 26

stem: A program sets a socket to non-blocking mode. When it calls `read()` and no data has arrived, the call returns immediately with `EAGAIN`, and the program loops back later to call `read()` again. Where does this fall in the synchronous/asynchronous × blocking/non-blocking matrix?

options.text: Synchronous and blocking, because the program calls read itself
options.why: Blocking would mean the call waits until data arrives; this one returns at once.

options.text: Synchronous and non-blocking
options.why: The caller still performs and polls the I/O itself, but no call waits.

options.text: Asynchronous and non-blocking, because the call returns at once
options.why: Asynchronous means the system completes the I/O and notifies you later.

options.text: Asynchronous and blocking, as it waits for EAGAIN
options.why: EAGAIN is returned without waiting, so nothing here blocks.

explanation: Blocking vs non-blocking is about whether a call waits. Synchronous vs asynchronous is about who completes the operation: in synchronous I/O the caller does the read itself (possibly after polling); in asynchronous I/O (such as POSIX AIO, io_uring completions or IOCP) the system performs it and signals completion. Polling a non-blocking descriptor is synchronous non-blocking.
reference: IBM developerWorks: 'Boost application performance using asynchronous I/O' (2×2 I/O model)

stem: Why is a context switch between two processes usually more expensive than a switch between two threads of the same process?

options.text: Processes have more registers to save than threads do
options.why: The register set is the same; the CPU state saved per switch is similar.

options.text: It changes the address space, losing TLB entries and cache warmth
options.why: Switching page tables invalidates (or tags) translations and the new process finds cold caches.

options.text: The kernel must copy the whole heap of the outgoing process
options.why: Memory is never copied on a switch; only page-table pointers change.

options.text: Process switches always happen only on a timer interrupt
options.why: Both kinds of switch can be triggered by blocking calls or the timer.

explanation: Both switches save and restore registers and run the scheduler. A process switch also loads a new page-table root, which flushes TLB entries unless the CPU tags them (PCID/ASID), and the incoming process usually finds its data missing from caches. Threads of one process keep the same address space, so these indirect costs are smaller.
reference: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, ch. 6 and 19 (TLBs)

stem: Put the steps of a preemptive context switch from thread T1 to thread T2 in order.

options.text: A timer interrupt fires while T1 is running in user mode
The kernel saves T1's registers into its kernel data structure
The scheduler picks T2 from the run queue
The kernel restores T2's registers (and address space if needed)
Return from the kernel resumes T2 in user mode

explanation: The timer interrupt traps into the kernel, which saves the running thread's context, asks the scheduler for the next runnable thread, loads that thread's context (switching page tables if it belongs to another process), and returns to user mode in the new thread.
reference: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)

stem: A service runs on 8 cores. Each request needs about 10 ms of CPU time and spends about 90 ms waiting on a downstream API. Using the rule threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute), roughly how many worker threads keep the CPUs busy?

options.text: 8, one per core
options.why: With 90% of each request spent waiting, 8 threads leave cores idle most of the time.

options.text: 16, two per core to cover hyper-threading
options.why: That ignores the wait-to-compute ratio, which is what sizes I/O-bound pools.

options.text: 80 threads, from 8 × (1 + 90 / 10)
720, so that every waiting request has a thread
options.why: 8 × 90 confuses the ratio with the raw wait time and badly oversubscribes the CPU.

explanation: For I/O-bound work each thread is busy only C/(W + C) of the time, so you need cores × (1 + W/C) threads to keep every core busy: 8 × (1 + 9) = 80. Treat the figure as a starting point and tune with measurements, since contention and memory also limit pool size.
reference: Goetz, Java Concurrency in Practice, §8.2

stem: On a CPU with 4 physical cores and simultaneous multithreading (8 logical CPUs), a CPU-bound workload runs about twice as fast with 8 threads as with 4.

options.text: True
options.why: Sibling hardware threads share each core's execution units and caches, so they do not double throughput.

options.text: False
options.why: SMT lets two threads share one core; gains are typically far below 2× and can be zero or negative for compute-heavy code.

explanation: Hyper-threading/SMT exposes two logical CPUs per core so that one thread can use execution units the other leaves idle, for example while it waits on memory. For tight compute loops both threads compete for the same units and caches, so the extra logical CPUs add much less than a full core.
reference: Intel: Hyper-Threading Technology overview

stem: A Go server easily runs 500,000 goroutines, but the same design with 500,000 OS threads fails. Which two reasons explain the difference? (Choose two.)

options.text: Goroutine stacks start at a few kilobytes and grow on demand
options.why: OS threads reserve a fixed stack (often around 1–8 MB of virtual memory) up front.

options.text: Goroutines are scheduled in user space onto a few OS threads
options.why: Switching between them avoids a kernel transition and kernel scheduler bookkeeping.

options.text: Goroutines run in parallel on all cores while threads cannot
options.why: OS threads run in parallel too; the difference is cost, not capability.

options.text: The kernel forbids more than one thread per CPU core
options.why: Kernels happily run far more threads than cores; they just pay for each one.

options.text: Goroutines never block, so they need no stack at all
options.why: Goroutines block often and do need stacks; theirs are just small and growable.

explanation: Go multiplexes many goroutines onto a small number of OS threads (M:N scheduling). Each goroutine costs a few kilobytes of stack that grows when needed, and switching between goroutines happens in the Go runtime, not the kernel. Half a million OS threads would need gigabytes of reserved stack and heavy kernel scheduling.
reference: Go FAQ: Why goroutines instead of threads?

stem: Thread A executes two atomic steps, a1 then a2. Thread B executes two atomic steps, b1 then b2. Each thread keeps its own order. How many different interleavings of the four steps are possible? Type a number.
explanation: Choose which 2 of the 4 time slots belong to A; the rest go to B, and each thread's order is fixed: C(4, 2) = 6. In general, threads with k1, k2, … steps have (k1 + k2 + …)! / (k1! × k2! × …) interleavings, which grows explosively and is why testing alone rarely finds every concurrency bug.
reference: Herlihy & Shavit, The Art of Multiprocessor Programming, ch. 1

stem: A job is 80% perfectly parallel and 20% serial. With 4 cores it runs 2.5× faster than on one core. Under Amdahl's law, how many cores are needed to reach a 4× speedup?

options.text: 8 cores, double the 4 that gave 2.5×
options.why: Speedup is not linear in cores once the serial part dominates.

options.text: 7 cores, by scaling 4 × 4 / 2.5 = 6.4 and rounding up
options.why: Proportional scaling ignores the fixed serial term.

options.text: 16 cores, since 0.8/n must fall to 0.05
It can never reach 4× because the ceiling is 4×
options.why: The ceiling is 1 / 0.2 = 5×, so 4× is reachable.

explanation: Set 1 / (0.2 + 0.8/n) = 4. Then 0.2 + 0.8/n = 0.25, so 0.8/n = 0.05 and n = 16. Going from 2.5× to 4× needs four times the cores, because every step closer to the 5× ceiling costs more hardware.
reference: Amdahl's law

stem: On a 64-core run, a simulation spends 5% of its wall time in serial setup and 95% in perfectly parallel work, and the team scales the problem size with the core count. What scaled speedup does Gustafson's law give, and how does it compare with Amdahl's prediction for the same fractions?

options.text: About 60.9×, far above Amdahl's ≈ 15.4× for a fixed-size problem
About 15.4× under both laws, because the fractions are identical
options.why: The laws answer different questions: fixed size vs growing size.

options.text: About 20×, the inverse of the 5% serial fraction
options.why: That is Amdahl's ceiling for a fixed-size problem, not Gustafson's scaled speedup.

options.text: Exactly 64×, since the parallel work grows with the cores
options.why: The serial 5% of the run still does not speed up.

explanation: Gustafson's law measures how much more work fits in the same time when the problem grows with the machine: S = s + p × n = 0.05 + 0.95 × 64 = 60.85. Amdahl's law fixes the problem size and asks how much faster it finishes: 1 / (0.05 + 0.95/64) ≈ 15.4. Which law applies depends on whether you need lower latency for the same job or more throughput on bigger jobs.
reference: Gustafson, 'Reevaluating Amdahl's Law' (1988)

stem: A team adds nodes to a cluster that keeps a shared cache coherent with point-to-point invalidation messages. Throughput rises up to about 30 nodes, then falls as more nodes are added. In the Universal Scalability Law, X(N) = N / (1 + σ(N − 1) + κN(N − 1)), which term explains the fall?

options.text: σ, the contention term for queueing on shared resources
options.why: Contention alone flattens throughput toward a ceiling; it never makes it fall.

options.text: κ, the coherency (crosstalk) term that grows with N²
options.why: Pairwise coordination grows quadratically, so past a peak each node costs more than it adds.

options.text: The serial fraction from Amdahl's law, applied per node
options.why: Amdahl predicts diminishing returns but never retrograde (falling) throughput.

options.text: The N in the numerator, once nodes exceed the core count
options.why: The numerator is ideal linear scaling; it only ever helps.

explanation: The USL has two penalties. σ models contention (waiting in line for a shared resource), which caps throughput like Amdahl's serial fraction. κ models coherency costs (every node exchanging data with every other), which grows with N(N − 1) and eventually makes throughput fall. Retrograde scaling is the signature of κ > 0.
reference: Gunther, Guerrilla Capacity Planning (Universal Scalability Law)

stem: A CPU-bound batch job ran fastest with 16 threads on a 16-core machine. Raising it to 64 threads made it slower. Which two effects explain the slowdown? (Choose two.)

options.text: Many more context switches as 64 runnable threads share 16 cores
options.why: Each switch costs direct time plus scheduler work, with no extra cores to use.

options.text: Threads evict each other's working sets from the caches
options.why: Oversubscribed threads keep reloading cold data after every switch.

options.text: Amdahl's law predicts a speedup below 1 beyond the core count
options.why: Amdahl never predicts slowdown; it only bounds the gain.

options.text: The OS stops preempting threads once there are more than cores
options.why: Preemption continues; that is exactly what causes the extra switches.

options.text: Each extra thread is pinned to the same core as the main thread
options.why: Schedulers spread threads across cores; nothing pins them by default.

explanation: Beyond the core count, extra CPU-bound threads add no execution capacity. They do add context switches, run-queue overhead and cache thrashing, because each thread finds its data evicted when it runs again. For CPU-bound work, size the pool to the number of cores.
reference: Goetz, Java Concurrency in Practice, §8.2

stem: An API handles 1,000 requests per second. Each request holds a database connection for 20 ms on average. The connection pool has 10 connections. What happens at peak load?

options.text: Nothing, since 10 connections cover 1,000 short requests easily
options.why: Little's law says 20 connections are busy on average, twice the pool.

options.text: Requests queue for connections: on average 20 are needed but only 10 exist
options.why: L = 1,000 × 0.02 = 20, so the pool caps throughput at 500 req/s.

options.text: The database slows down, so each request holds its connection for 10 ms instead
options.why: Hold time does not shrink to fit the pool; queueing adds to it.

options.text: Throughput rises to 1,000 req/s once the pool warms up
options.why: With 10 connections × 50 uses per second each, the ceiling is 500 req/s.

explanation: Little's law: L = λW = 1,000 × 0.02 = 20 connections in use on average. A pool of 10 can serve at most 10 / 0.02 = 500 requests per second, so at 1,000 req/s requests wait for a connection and latency grows without bound until load drops or the pool grows.
reference: Little's law; HikariCP: About Pool Sizing

stem: On JDK 21, a server uses virtual threads. Each request enters a `synchronized` block and then makes a blocking network call inside it. Under load, throughput is far lower than expected. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Virtual threads cannot perform blocking network I/O at all
options.why: Blocking I/O is exactly what virtual threads are designed to handle cheaply.

options.text: Blocking inside synchronized pins the virtual thread to its carrier
options.why: A pinned virtual thread keeps its platform thread busy, so few requests can wait at once.

options.text: synchronized blocks are skipped entirely by virtual threads
options.why: Synchronization semantics are unchanged; only the blocking behaviour differs.

options.text: The JVM creates one carrier thread per virtual thread by default
options.why: Carriers come from a small ForkJoinPool, roughly one per core.

explanation: JEP 444 (JDK 21): a virtual thread is pinned to its carrier while it runs inside a synchronized block or a native method, so blocking there ties up the platform thread. With only about one carrier per core, a few pinned threads exhaust them. Fixes on JDK 21 are using ReentrantLock instead of synchronized around blocking calls; JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed this pinning for synchronized.
reference: JEP 444: Virtual Threads; JEP 491

stem: In Go, a goroutine makes a blocking system call (for example a read from a regular file). With GOMAXPROCS=4, what happens to the other runnable goroutines?

options.text: They stall until the syscall returns, since its P is held
options.why: Go deliberately avoids this by detaching the P from the blocked thread.

options.text: The runtime hands the P to another OS thread so they keep running
options.why: The blocked M keeps the goroutine; its P moves on to a new or idle M.

options.text: GOMAXPROCS is raised to 5 for the duration of the call
options.why: GOMAXPROCS stays at 4; the runtime just uses an extra M.

options.text: The goroutine is converted to non-blocking I/O automatically
options.why: Regular-file reads really block the thread; only network I/O uses the poller.

explanation: Go's scheduler has G (goroutines), M (OS threads) and P (processors, numbering GOMAXPROCS). When a goroutine blocks its M in a syscall, the runtime takes the P off that M and attaches it to another M, so 4 Ps keep running Go code. This is why a Go program may have more OS threads than GOMAXPROCS.
reference: Go runtime scheduler (runtime/proc.go design notes)

stem: An asyncio service handles thousands of requests concurrently. One handler computes a large hash in a pure-Python loop that takes 2 seconds and never awaits. What happens to every other request during those 2 seconds?

options.text: They all stall, because the event loop cannot switch until it yields
options.why: Coroutine scheduling is cooperative; a task that never awaits monopolises the loop.

options.text: They continue, because the loop preempts tasks every few milliseconds
options.why: asyncio has no preemption; switches happen only at await points.

options.text: They continue on other cores, since asyncio runs one task per core
options.why: An asyncio loop runs on one thread; tasks share it.

options.text: Only requests to the same endpoint stall, others are unaffected
options.why: All tasks on the loop share one thread, whatever the endpoint.

explanation: Cooperative scheduling only switches tasks when the running one yields (await). CPU-heavy code with no awaits blocks the whole loop, so every timer, socket and request waits. Offload such work with loop.run_in_executor or asyncio.to_thread, or to a process pool for real CPU parallelism.
reference: Python docs: asyncio — Developing with asyncio (Running blocking code)

stem: Match each description with its quadrant in the I/O model matrix.

options.text: Synchronous, blocking
Synchronous, non-blocking
Asynchronous, blocking
Asynchronous, non-blocking

prompts.text: A plain read() on a blocking socket that waits until data arrives
Repeatedly calling read() on a non-blocking socket until it stops returning EAGAIN
Waiting in select() or epoll_wait() for readiness, then calling read()
Submitting a read to io_uring and later reaping its completion

explanation: The classic 2×2 I/O model separates waiting (blocking vs non-blocking) from who completes the operation (synchronous vs asynchronous). I/O multiplexing with select/epoll is usually classed as asynchronous blocking: the program blocks in the readiness call, not in the I/O itself. Completion-based APIs such as io_uring, IOCP and POSIX AIO are asynchronous non-blocking.
reference: IBM developerWorks: 'Boost application performance using asynchronous I/O'

stem: Which two designs keep a crash in one unit of work (for example a segmentation fault in a native library) from taking down unrelated units? (Choose two.)

options.text: Running each unit in its own OS process
options.why: Process boundaries isolate memory, so one crash ends only that process.

options.text: Erlang/BEAM processes supervised and restarted by a supervisor
options.why: BEAM processes share nothing, and supervisors restart failed ones.

options.text: Running each unit in its own thread of one process
options.why: A segfault in any thread kills the whole process.

options.text: Running each unit as a goroutine with a deferred recover()
options.why: recover catches Go panics, not segmentation faults in native code.

options.text: Giving each unit its own asyncio task on one loop
options.why: All tasks share one process and thread, so a hard crash kills them all.

explanation: Isolation needs separate address spaces or a runtime that enforces share-nothing semantics. OS processes (as in PostgreSQL backends or browser site isolation) contain native crashes. BEAM processes share no memory, and supervisors restart failures. Threads, goroutines and coroutines share one address space, so a native crash anywhere takes down the whole process.
reference: Erlang/OTP docs: Supervisor behaviour

stem: On a two-socket NUMA server, one thread allocates and initialises a 20 GB array, then a pool of threads spread over both sockets processes it. Threads on socket 1 run noticeably slower than those on socket 0. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Socket 1 has fewer cores, so its threads wait longer for the CPU
options.why: Both sockets usually have the same cores; the issue is memory locality.

options.text: First-touch put all pages on socket 0, so socket 1 reads remote memory
options.why: Linux places pages on the node that first touches them; remote accesses cross the interconnect.

options.text: The array is too large for the L1 cache on socket 1
options.why: L1 is tiny on every core; it does not explain a per-socket difference.

options.text: Socket 1 threads must lock the array before every access
options.why: Nothing in the scenario adds locking; the slowdown is memory distance.

explanation: With the default first-touch policy, a page lives on the NUMA node of the thread that first writes it. One thread initialising everything puts the whole array on its own node, so the other socket's threads pay remote-memory latency and share interconnect bandwidth. Fix it with parallel first-touch initialisation, interleaved allocation (numactl --interleave) or by pinning threads near their data.
reference: Linux kernel docs: NUMA memory policy

stem: Three threads each execute two atomic steps in program order, and the scheduler may interleave them in any way. How many distinct interleavings are possible? Type a number.
explanation: The count is 6! / (2! × 2! × 2!) = 720 / 8 = 90. Adding one more two-step thread gives 8! / 2⁴ = 2,520. The state space explodes so fast that concurrency bugs often hide in rare interleavings that ordinary testing never hits.
reference: Herlihy & Shavit, The Art of Multiprocessor Programming, ch. 1

stem: Order these latencies from fastest to slowest on typical server hardware.

options.text: L1 cache hit
Last-level (L3) cache hit
Local DRAM access
Remote-NUMA-node DRAM access
NVMe SSD random read
Network round trip within one data centre

explanation: Roughly: L1 ~1 ns, L3 ~10–40 ns, local DRAM ~80–100 ns, remote NUMA DRAM ~1.5–2× local, NVMe random read ~10–100 µs, and an in-datacentre round trip ~100–500 µs. Each step is roughly an order of magnitude, which is why cache-friendly data layout and locality matter so much for parallel code.
reference: Dean, 'Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know'

stem: A pure 1:N green-thread runtime schedules many user-level threads on a single kernel thread, without help from the kernel. Which three statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Switching between green threads needs no kernel transition
options.why: The runtime saves and restores context in user space.

options.text: One green thread making a blocking syscall blocks all of them
options.why: The kernel sees one thread; when it blocks, nothing else can run.

options.text: All green threads together can use at most one CPU core
options.why: There is only one kernel thread for the OS to schedule.

options.text: The kernel preempts each green thread with its own timer
options.why: The kernel does not know green threads exist.

options.text: Each green thread has its own kernel thread ID
options.why: They all share the single kernel thread's identity.

options.text: A crash in one green thread leaves the others running
options.why: They share one process, so a crash takes them all down.

explanation: Pure user-level (1:N) threading is cheap to switch but invisible to the kernel: a blocking call stalls everything and there is no multicore parallelism. M:N designs such as Go's scheduler and Java virtual threads fix this by running many user-level threads on several kernel threads and handing off around blocking calls.
reference: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, ch. 27 (Thread API) and threading models

stem: A logging pipeline sends events to storage in batches: it flushes when 100 events have accumulated or 50 ms have passed, whichever comes first. Compared with writing each event individually, what is the main trade-off?

options.text: Both throughput and latency improve, with no downside
options.why: Waiting to fill a batch adds delay to the first events in it.

options.text: Higher throughput per write, at the cost of up to 50 ms added latency
options.why: Fewer, larger writes amortise overhead while events wait for the batch.

options.text: Lower throughput, because batches must be serialised first
options.why: Batching amortises per-call overhead, so throughput usually rises.

options.text: Latency drops because storage handles batches faster
options.why: An individual event can only wait longer, never less, for its batch.

explanation: Batching trades latency for throughput: per-write overhead (syscalls, network round trips, fsyncs) is shared by many events, but each event may wait until the batch fills or the timer fires. The size and time caps bound the extra latency. This is the same trade-off as Nagle's algorithm or group commit.
reference: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, ch. 1 (Throughput vs latency)

stem: Order these operations from cheapest to most expensive in typical cost of switching or invoking.

options.text: An ordinary function call
Switching between two goroutines or coroutines in user space
Switching between two threads of the same process
Switching between two threads in different processes

explanation: A function call is a few nanoseconds. A user-space coroutine switch saves a handful of registers without entering the kernel (tens to low hundreds of ns). A thread switch enters the kernel and runs the scheduler (around a microsecond or more). A cross-process switch adds an address-space change, TLB effects and colder caches.
reference: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, ch. 6

stem: A job's single-core runtime splits into three parts: 20% strictly serial, 30% that scales to at most 4 workers, and 50% that scales perfectly. What speedup does it reach on 16 cores?

options.why: That treats the 30% section as if it scaled to 16 cores.

options.text: About 3.3×, since runtime drops to 0.306
About 5×, the serial ceiling of 1 / 0.2
options.why: 5× is the limit with infinite cores and perfect scaling of all non-serial work.

options.text: About 2.5×, because the capped section limits everything to 4 cores
options.why: Only the 30% section is capped; the 50% section still uses all 16.

explanation: Generalised Amdahl: add up each section's time at its own achievable parallelism. Serial: 0.2. Capped section: 0.3 / 4 = 0.075. Fully parallel: 0.5 / 16 = 0.03125. Total 0.30625, so speedup = 1 / 0.30625 ≈ 3.27. Partially parallel sections act like extra serial work once cores exceed their limit.
reference: Amdahl's law (multi-section form)

stem: A system follows the Universal Scalability Law with contention σ = 0.05 and coherency κ = 0.001. Roughly how many nodes give peak throughput?

options.text: About 20 nodes, the inverse of σ
options.why: 1/σ is a contention-only ceiling on speedup, not the node count of the peak.

options.text: About 1,000 nodes, the inverse of κ
options.why: The peak depends on the square root of the ratio, not on 1/κ.

options.text: About 31 nodes, near √((1 − σ) / κ)
There is no peak; throughput rises forever toward 20×
options.why: With κ > 0 throughput peaks and then declines.

explanation: For X(N) = N / (1 + σ(N − 1) + κN(N − 1)), throughput peaks at N* = √((1 − σ) / κ) = √(0.95 / 0.001) ≈ 30.8. At 31 nodes the relative capacity is about 9.0×; at 64 nodes it drops to about 7.8×, so adding nodes past the peak actually costs throughput.
reference: Gunther, Guerrilla Capacity Planning

stem: A service with a fixed pool of 64 worker threads makes one blocking downstream call per request, taking 200 ms. Load rises to 500 requests per second. What happens, and why?

options.text: It handles the load, since 64 threads × 5 calls each covers 500 req/s
options.why: 64 threads at 5 calls per second each give only 320 req/s.

options.text: It caps at 320 req/s, so the queue and latency grow without bound
options.why: Little's law needs 500 × 0.2 = 100 concurrent workers; only 64 exist.

options.text: Latency stays at 200 ms but 36% of requests are rejected immediately
options.why: Unbounded queues delay requests rather than rejecting them.

options.text: It handles 500 req/s, because CPUs sit idle during the blocking calls
options.why: Idle CPUs do not help when every thread is occupied waiting.

explanation: Little's law: concurrency needed = λW = 500 × 0.2 = 100, but the pool supplies 64, so maximum throughput is 64 / 0.2 = 320 req/s. With arrivals above service capacity, an unbounded queue grows forever and latency climbs until timeouts or memory exhaustion. Fixes are a larger pool, non-blocking I/O or virtual threads, a bounded queue with load shedding, or a faster downstream.
reference: Little's law

stem: A team plans to adopt Java virtual threads. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: They suit high-concurrency workloads that mostly block on I/O
options.why: Cheap blocking lets one thread per request scale to many concurrent requests.

options.text: They should not be pooled; create one per task instead
options.why: They are cheap enough that pooling adds overhead and defeats their purpose.

options.text: They make CPU-bound computations finish faster
options.why: They add no CPU capacity; CPU-bound work is still limited by cores.

options.text: They remove the need for synchronisation on shared data
options.why: They are still threads; shared mutable state still needs synchronisation.

options.text: Each virtual thread gets its own dedicated OS thread
options.why: Many virtual threads share a small pool of carrier platform threads.

explanation: JEP 444 positions virtual threads for the thread-per-request style with high concurrency and mostly blocking I/O. They are cheap to create, so you spawn one per task rather than pooling them; to limit concurrency to a scarce resource, use a Semaphore. They do not make computation faster, and normal thread-safety rules still apply.
reference: JEP 444: Virtual Threads

stem: Two CPU-bound threads that each saturate a core are placed on the two hardware threads (SMT siblings) of one physical core, while three other physical cores sit idle. How should they be scheduled for best throughput?

options.text: Keep them as siblings, since SMT doubles each core's throughput
options.why: Siblings share execution units and caches, so two compute threads slow each other.

options.text: Spread them onto separate physical cores
options.why: Each then has a full core's execution units and caches to itself.

options.text: Pin both to the same logical CPU so they share its cache fully
options.why: They would then time-share one hardware thread, which is worse still.

options.text: Disable SMT, since sibling threads always reduce total throughput
options.why: SMT often helps mixed or stall-heavy workloads; the fix here is placement.

explanation: SMT siblings share one core's execution resources and private caches. Two compute-heavy threads on siblings compete for the same units, while separate physical cores give each its own. Modern schedulers try to fill physical cores before siblings, but pinning or affinity masks can override that, which is a common self-inflicted slowdown.
reference: Intel: Hyper-Threading Technology overview

stem: A Go 1.22 program runs with GOMAXPROCS=1. One goroutine spins in `for {}` with no function calls. Can the other goroutines still run?

options.text: No, the spinning goroutine never reaches a safe point to yield
options.why: That was true before Go 1.14, when preemption happened only at function calls.

options.text: Yes, the runtime preempts it asynchronously and schedules others
options.why: Since Go 1.14 goroutines are asynchronously preemptible, even in tight loops.

options.text: Only the garbage collector runs; user goroutines stay blocked
options.why: Preemption lets the scheduler run any runnable goroutine, not only GC.

options.text: Yes, because GOMAXPROCS=1 still creates one thread per goroutine
options.why: GOMAXPROCS=1 means one P; other goroutines need preemption to get it.

explanation: Before Go 1.14 the scheduler preempted goroutines only at function-call safe points, so a call-free loop could hog a P and stall the scheduler and GC. Go 1.14 added asynchronous preemption using signals, so tight loops are preempted too. With GOMAXPROCS=1 the others still share one P, so the spinner wastes CPU, but they are no longer starved.
reference: Go 1.14 release notes (Runtime)

stem: An Erlang system runs 200,000 lightweight processes. One of them builds a very large data structure and triggers a long garbage collection. Why do the other processes keep serving requests without a global pause?

options.text: The BEAM collects garbage only when the whole node is idle
options.why: GC runs whenever a process needs it, not only at idle times.

options.text: Each process has its own heap and is collected independently
options.why: GC of one process heap does not stop the processes that own other heaps.

options.text: Erlang has no garbage collector; memory is freed on process exit
options.why: Erlang does garbage-collect live processes, per process.

options.text: The BEAM runs the collector on a GPU so CPUs are not paused
options.why: There is no GPU offload; per-process heaps are what isolate the pause.

explanation: BEAM processes share nothing: each has a private heap collected by a per-process generational collector, while large binaries live in a shared reference-counted area. A big collection pauses only the process that owns that heap, and the reduction-based preemptive scheduler keeps other processes running on all schedulers.
reference: Erlang docs: Garbage collector (erts) and processes

stem: Under the C10K problem, why does a classic thread-per-connection server struggle with 10,000 mostly idle keep-alive connections? (Choose two.)

options.text: Each idle connection still holds a thread with its stack and kernel state
options.why: Memory and kernel structures scale with connections, not with actual work.

options.text: Thousands of threads add scheduler and context-switch overhead
options.why: Wake-ups and switches across many threads waste CPU when little work is done.

options.text: The kernel limits each process to 1,024 threads
options.why: Thread limits are configurable and far higher; memory runs out first.

options.text: TCP cannot keep more than 1,024 connections open per port
options.why: A listening port accepts far more connections; limits come from file descriptors and memory.

options.text: Threads cannot wait on sockets, only on files
options.why: Threads can block on sockets; doing it 10,000 times is just expensive.

explanation: The C10K problem (Dan Kegel, 1999) observed that one thread or process per connection wastes memory and scheduling effort when most connections are idle. Event-driven servers instead multiplex many sockets on a few threads using readiness or completion APIs (epoll, kqueue, IOCP), which nginx and Node.js popularised. The later C10M framing pushes further into kernel-bypass designs.
reference: Kegel, 'The C10K problem'

stem: A container has a CPU limit of 2 cores on a 64-core node. The application sizes its worker pool from the host core count and starts 64 CPU-bound workers. Latency spikes under load. Which two changes address the root cause? (Choose two.)

options.text: Size the worker pool from the container's CPU quota (about 2)
options.why: Matching workers to available CPU stops 64 workers fighting over 2 cores.

options.text: Tell the runtime the real CPU budget, e.g. GOMAXPROCS or -XX:ActiveProcessorCount
options.why: Runtimes that size thread pools from visible CPUs then pick sensible defaults.

options.text: Raise the memory limit so workers have more room
options.why: Memory is not the bottleneck; CPU quota throttling is.

options.text: Lower the process nice value inside the container
options.why: Priority within the container does not create more CPU quota.

options.text: Disable SMT on the node so each worker gets a full core
options.why: The container can still only use 2 cores of quota, whatever the topology.

explanation: A CPU limit is enforced by the CFS bandwidth controller as a time quota per period. Sixty-four busy workers burn through a 2-core quota early in each period and are then throttled until the next one, producing latency spikes. Size pools to the quota and make sure the runtime sees the real budget: some runtimes detect cgroup limits automatically, others need GOMAXPROCS, -XX:ActiveProcessorCount or similar.
reference: Linux kernel docs: CFS Bandwidth Control

stem: Two threads each run `r = x; x = r + 1` on a shared `x` that starts at 0. The read and the write are each atomic, but the pair is not. Of the 6 possible interleavings, how many leave `x` equal to 2?

options.text: All 6, because each thread adds 1
options.why: Overlapping reads can both see 0 and both write 1.

options.text: 4 of them
options.why: Four interleavings actually lose an update and end at 1.

options.text: 2 of them
options.why: Only when one thread finishes both steps before the other reads.

options.text: None, since the writes always overwrite each other
options.why: Sequential executions do produce 2.

explanation: Enumerating the 6 interleavings: x ends at 2 only for A-read, A-write, B-read, B-write and the mirror order. In the other 4, both threads read 0 before either writes, so the second write overwrites the first and x ends at 1. This lost update is why read-modify-write sequences need atomic operations or locks.
reference: Herlihy & Shavit, The Art of Multiprocessor Programming, ch. 1

stem: A search team must decide which scaling law to use when justifying a move from 32 to 256 nodes. Their goal is to answer a single query 8× faster on the same index. Which statement is right?

options.text: Gustafson's law applies, since more nodes always process more data
options.why: Gustafson assumes the problem grows with the machine; here it is fixed.

options.text: Amdahl's law applies, because the problem size stays fixed
options.why: Reducing latency for a fixed job is exactly Amdahl's question.

options.text: Little's law applies, because it relates nodes to throughput
options.why: Little's law relates concurrency, throughput and time in queue, not speedup.

options.text: Neither applies to distributed systems, only to multicore CPUs
options.why: Both laws apply to any parallel system, distributed or not.

explanation: Amdahl's law answers "how much faster does this fixed-size job finish with n workers?" and is the right model for single-query latency. Gustafson's law answers "how much more work fits in the same time if the job grows with n?" and suits throughput on larger datasets. With any non-trivial serial share (query planning, merging results), 8× fewer seconds from 8× more nodes is unlikely.
reference: Amdahl's law; Gustafson's law

stem: A 16-core server targets 75% CPU utilisation. Each task needs 5 ms of CPU and then waits 45 ms on I/O. Using threads = cores × target utilisation × (1 + wait/compute), how many threads should the pool have? Type a number.
explanation: 16 × 0.75 × (1 + 45/5) = 16 × 0.75 × 10 = 120. The formula from Java Concurrency in Practice scales the core count by the desired utilisation and by how much of each task is spent waiting. Validate it under real load, since locks, memory and downstream limits can make the true optimum lower.
reference: Goetz, Java Concurrency in Practice, §8.2

stem: In the Universal Scalability Law, a system with no contention (σ = 0) but any positive coherency cost (κ > 0) will eventually lose throughput as more nodes are added.

options.text: True
options.why: With σ = 0, X(N) = N / (1 + κN(N − 1)) peaks near N = √(1/κ) and then falls.

options.text: False
options.why: The quadratic κ term outgrows the linear numerator, whatever σ is.

explanation: With σ = 0 the denominator is 1 + κN(N − 1), which grows quadratically while the numerator grows linearly. For κ = 0.001 throughput peaks at about √1000 ≈ 32 nodes (≈ 16×) and drops to ≈ 13× at 60 nodes. Coherency alone is enough to cause retrograde scaling.
reference: Gunther, Guerrilla Capacity Planning

stem: Match each performance symptom with the most likely underlying cause.

options.text: Contention on a shared resource (USL σ)
Coherency or crosstalk costs (USL κ)
Oversubscription with too many runnable threads
Queueing as utilisation approaches 100%

prompts.text: Throughput flattens at a ceiling as nodes are added but never falls
Throughput peaks, then drops as more nodes join
CPU is busy, yet much of it goes to context switching and cache misses
Latency explodes while throughput barely rises as load nears capacity

explanation: A plateau points to a serialised bottleneck (σ). Retrograde scaling points to pairwise coordination (κ). Lots of runnable threads with poor useful work points to oversubscription. Latency that shoots up near full utilisation is basic queueing theory: in an M/M/1 queue, response time grows like 1 / (1 − ρ) as utilisation ρ → 1.
reference: Gunther, Guerrilla Capacity Planning; Kleinrock, Queueing Systems
